Article Title: ‘They lack courage as we are Maharana Pratap descendants’: BJP MLA claims Pakistan-based group threatened to kill him
Article Text:
BJP MLA Nand Kishor Gurjar claimed that he received a threat from Pakistan based organisation

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party MLA from Uttar Pradesh's Loni Nand Kishor Gurjar on Sunday claimed to have received a death threat from a Pakistan-based organisation.Gurjar claimed that he received a call from a Pakistan-based organisation, which threatened to bomb his house and kill him."I received a call in the morning from a Pakistan-based organisation, which threatened to bomb my house and kill me. I told them that they do not have the courage to do so," the BJP MLA claimed."We are descendants of Maharana Pratap and Chhatrapati Shivaji, and we will deal with them," he added.Gurjar also said that Pakistan was on the brink of starvation and that India had become a country that responds firmly under the leadership of PM Modi."Pakistan is on the brink of starvation. Under the leadership of PM Modi, India has become a country that responds firmly after centuries of being subjected to attacks," he said."Our armed forces have demonstrated this through surgical strikes," he added.This comes after a blast at a police outpost in Ghaziabad left one person injured on Saturday.Police are verifying a social media post by an organisation named "Tehrik Ul Mujahideen", which has claimed responsibility for the blast that occurred late Friday night. The explosion damaged the window panes of the Vasundhara police outpost under the Indirapuram police station.The explosion occurred near the police outpost's boundary wall, police said.The intensity and motive behind the blast are yet to be ascertained, but police have indicated that the probe will include a possible terrorist angle.
Article Summary: Bharatiya Janata Party MLA from Uttar Pradesh's Loni Nand Kishor Gurjar on Sunday claimed to have received a death threat from a Pakistan-based organisation. Gurjar said that Pakistan was on the brink of starvation and that India had become a country that responds firmly under the leadership of PM Modi.

Article Title: 'Karnataka needs no permission for Mekedatu': DK Shivakumar on Tamil Nadu CM Vijay's letter to PM Modi

NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Sunday asserted that there is "no need of permission" to build the Mekedatu reservoir across the Cauvery river, which has been at the centre of a long-standing water-sharing dispute between Karnataka and neighbouring Tamil Nadu.Shivakumar's remarks came after his Tamil Nadu counteprart C Joseph Vijay wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In his letter, Vijay urged PM Modi to ensure that Karnataka is not granted any clearance to construct the Mekedatu dam without the consent of the other Cauvery basin states, including Tamil Nadu."I hope that Tamil Nadu's chief minister know the law of the land. No need of permission from anyone. The Supreme Court has already given permission that Karnataka is eligible to build the dam on its own site. And it has put a condition that we should give them 177 TMC of water. That is the condition," ANI quoted the Karnataka chief minister as saying.Shivakumar claimed that the Mekedatu reservoir would ultimately benefit Tamil Nadu more than Karnataka."Tamil Nadu will have more benefit from the Mekedatu reservoir. Balance it is called a balancing reservoir," he said.He further said that Karnataka had identified 5,400 hectares of forest land for compensatory afforestation to meet environmental requirements.The process is underway, after which the state will approach the water commission for clearance.Shivakumar reassured Vijay that Karnataka would honour its commitments and not misuse the water stored in the reservoir."I appeal to the Tamil Nadu chief minister; please send a team. We will not misuse this. We stand by our word," he stated.He furher called for cooperation between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, saying the two states should respect the Supreme Court's verdict and work together on water-sharing issues."There's no question of fighting. The fighting days are over. The Supreme Court has given a verdict. Let us respect the law of this land. Let us work together. Let us share water," he added.He also highlighted the Cauvery's importance for drinking water, agriculture, livestock and industries in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Kerala.Describing the Cauvery basin as a gift to the country, Shivakumar urged Vijay to strengthen ties between the states and work towards farmers' welfare.
Article Summary: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar says there is "no need of permission" to build the Mekedatu reservoir across the Cauvery river. Tamil Nadu counteprart C Joseph Vijay wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Vijay urged PM Modi to ensure that Karnataka is not granted any clearance to construct the dam.

Article Title: 'Will remain indebted to their valour': Rajnath Singh pays homage to immortal bravehearts in Sikkim
Article Text:
Rajnath Singh pays tribute to fallen soldiers at Sikkim's Sherathang War Memorial on Diwali

NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday paid tribute to fallen soldiers at the Sherathang War Memorial in Sikkim on the occasion of Diwali, saying the nation would "always remain indebted to their valor".Singh also met and interacted with troops deployed in the challenging sector, praising their commitment and morale despite extreme weather conditions and difficult terrain.Sharing details of his visit on X, the defence minister said the soldiers' supreme sacrifice in the line of duty would remain etched in the memory of the nation."On the auspicious occasion of Diwali today, paid homage to our immortal bravehearts at the Sherathang War Memorial in Sikkim. As the saying goes, 'Monuments are for the living, not the dead'-they stand to continuously inspire us and awaken our national pride. Their supreme sacrifice in the line of duty will forever remain etched in the memory of a grateful nation, and we will always remain indebted to their valor," he said.Describing the troops as "diyas" who silently fight darkness and spread the light of security across the country, Singh said their unflinching vigil and patriotism burn brighter than a thousand lamps."Also had the honor of meeting and interacting with our courageous troops deployed in this forward and challenging sector. Our jawans are like 'diyas' themselves, silently fighting the darkness and spreading the light of security to every home in the country. Even in extreme weather and difficult terrain, their unflinching vigil, boundless patriotism, and high morale burn brighter than a thousand lamps," he said."It is a matter of profound pride to celebrate Diwali among the true guardians of the motherland. Wishing all our brave personnel serving on the borders and their families a very Happy and Prosperous Diwali," he added.
Article Summary: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday paid tribute to fallen soldiers at the Sherathang War Memorial in Sikkim. He said the nation would "always remain indebted to their valor" Singh also met and interacted with troops deployed in the challenging sector.

Article Title: 'Armed Naxals wiped out, but threat not over': PM Modi warns of 'Dimagi Naxals' in political parties
Article Text:
PM Modi said the country needed to identify and defeat such elements to ensure national security

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said that while armed Naxalites had been eliminated from the forests, the threat of Naxalism was not over, claiming that "Dimagi Naxals" had taken control of several organisations including political parties.Addressing security personnel while celebrating Diwali at a Central Reserve Police Force ( CRPF ) camp in Karanpur in Chhattisgarh's Bastar district, PM Modi said the country needed to identify and defeat such elements to ensure national security."We must remember one thing. Naxalites have been eliminated, but the threat is not yet over. While armed Naxalites have been wiped out from the forests, 'Dimagi Naxals' have taken control of several organisations. Even today, they are inciting people against the country's Constitution and democracy. These 'Dimagi Naxals' have also infiltrated several political parties and different organisations. We must identify them, defeat them and ensure the security of the nation," he said.The prime minister's remarks come months after the Centre announced on March 31 that the country had been freed from the menace of Naxalism following the elimination of several Maoist leaders and cadres and the surrender of hundreds of others.PM Modi described the elimination of Maoist terror as a victory for the government's policies and political will. He said his government had taken decisions that dealt a major blow to the funding networks of Naxalites and separatists, while giving security forces greater freedom to respond to attacks."Earlier governments had tied the hands of security forces in the fight on the ground. Maoist attacks took place, but security forces did not have the freedom to retaliate effectively. We gave security forces the freedom to take all necessary decisions," he said.He also said the government had worked to dismantle the support networks that Left-Wing Extremism received from within the administration and the system.PM Modi said the government's objective was to ensure that no family lost a child to Maoist violence and no young person was forced to take up arms. He added that sustained security operations, alongside development initiatives, had helped win the trust of people in Naxal-affected areas.Recalling the scale of the challenge, the prime minister said more than 230 districts across nearly 20 states had once been affected by Naxalism. He also pointed out that, for the first time in 47 years, not a single CRPF personnel had been killed in the line of duty over the past year.
Article Summary: PM Modi said the country needed to identify and defeat such elements to ensure national security. The Centre announced on March 31 that the country had been freed from the menace of Naxalism. PM Modi described the elimination of Maoist terror as a victory for the government's policies and political will.

Article Title: Abhishek Banerjee's birthday turns into BJP-TMC showdown in Bengal: What we know
Article Text:
TMC Chief Mamata Banerjee addresses a press conference, in New Delhi on Thursday. TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee also present.

Mamata joins protest, writes to Lok Sabha Speaker

What happened outside Abhishek’s residence

Abhishek alleges two-day surveillance, attack plot

Abhishek accuses police of inaction

What police said

BJP rejects charges, blames birthday gathering

TMC leaders allege planned attack; opposition voices concern

Political tensions in Bengal

NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee joined Trinamool Congress (TMC) national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee in a protest in Kolkata’s Kalighat. She accused the BJP of hooliganism and alleged a breakdown of law and order in the state.She said she had written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over the incident.The protest followed an overnight confrontation outside Abhishek’s residence, where clashes reportedly broke out between TMC workers and BJP supporters around 2am. Abhishek alleged that BJP workers attacked his residence after conducting reconnaissance of the premises for two days.He later claimed that the confrontation continued until 7am, accused police personnel of failing to stop the attackers and alleged that some officers were assaulted while trying to intervene. Several people were reportedly injured, while police imposed prohibitory restrictions around the residence and detained some people.BJP rejected the allegations, blaming the confrontation on a birthday gathering organised on a public road.The incident has since triggered a political war of words, with leaders from both sides trading accusations over the violence and the state’s law-and-order situation.Mamata reached Abhishek’s Kalighat residence later on Saturday and joined the protest. She accused the BJP of creating disturbances in the area and alleged that a group of people had attacked a Kali Puja celebration.She also raised concerns over the arrangements for traditional pujas ahead of Kali Puja and Diwali. Mamata claimed that permissions for some long-standing puja celebrations had been revoked while a new puja was allowed to be organised on the main road.“Tomorrow is Kali Puja and Diwali. Last night, at 2:00 AM, an attack was carried out at Abhishek Banerjee’s house. This is our locality, a route through which many processions of Goddess Kali pass. Why are you causing such a disturbance? You have revoked permissions for our traditional, long-standing pujas while allowing new ones to be held instead,” she said.She alleged that the new puja arrangement had blocked access to their own celebration and accused the authorities of high-handedness. She also said she had written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over what she described as a breakdown of law and order.The confrontation reportedly began around 2am on Saturday, when BJP supporters allegedly raised slogans calling Abhishek a “chor” (thief) outside his Kalighat residence. TMC workers had gathered in the area. According to reports, the slogans were followed by counter-sloganeering, arguments and a clash between the two groups.The confrontation involved allegations of assault, stone-pelting and vandalism. Abhishek, who came out of his residence during the night to meet injured party workers, alleged that the attackers used wooden rods fitted with nails and vandalised a local TMC office.Police and party accounts put the duration of the initial clashes between 2am and 3.30am. Abhishek, however, later claimed that the confrontation continued until 7am.He alleged that four to five of his supporters sustained serious injuries. One of them, he said, required plastic surgery, while another suffered a fracture. Police sources said several people from both sides were injured. A separate report put the number of injured at eight, including three who were seriously hurt.The incident came hours after Abhishek raised allegations of surveillance outside his office and residence. On Friday, he claimed that unidentified individuals had been conducting reconnaissance of the premises for two consecutive days.He said the individuals claimed to be police personnel when confronted. Abhishek questioned why the state police were allegedly keeping watch on an elected MP’s residence and demanded an inquiry into who had authorised the surveillance and for what purpose.He tagged Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, Kolkata Police, West Bengal Police and the Union Home Ministry in his post, seeking an investigation to establish the identities of those involved.Hours later, he alleged that his residence had been attacked by BJP workers. Sharing a video purportedly showing the incident, he wrote on X: “After two days of continuous recce, this is how BJP hooligans attacked my house at 2 am today. Watch the footage and see for yourself. If this is what can happen to an elected Member of Parliament, imagine the plight of the common man in WB.”PTI said it could not independently verify the authenticity of the video.Abhishek described the incident as the seventh attempt on his life in six months. He also accused the police and the judiciary of failing to act against those allegedly targeting him.Escalating his criticism after the confrontation, Abhishek alleged that police personnel present at the spot failed to prevent the violence. He claimed that some officers remained silent spectators, while others who tried to intervene were assaulted.“The attack continued till 7 am. Although the police were there, some of them acted as silent spectators, and others who tried to stop the BJP goons were beaten up by them,” he said.“The police who can’t protect themselves cannot protect the common people anyway,” he added.Abhishek also shared a video that he claimed showed a BJP worker slapping a plainclothes police officer. The TMC accused the BJP workers of assaulting police personnel and questioned why those involved had not been arrested.He said the incident showed how vulnerable ordinary people could be if police personnel themselves were unable to protect themselves. He also cited figures on alleged crimes in the state between May and October, claiming that around 2,500 rapes, 600 murders and more than 32,000 crimes had taken place during the period. These figures were claims made by Abhishek.The Kolkata Police said a commotion had broken out between supporters of the two parties and that a police team intervened. An investigation was underway, a police officer said, without providing further details.Prohibitory orders were imposed around Abhishek’s residence, barring gatherings of more than five people. A large police contingent was deployed in the area and several people were detained in connection with the incident.Police sources said people from both sides had been injured and the situation remained tense through the night.The BJP rejected Abhishek’s allegations and accused TMC supporters of provoking the confrontation by holding a birthday celebration on a public road.West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh dismissed the claims as an attempt to mislead people. He questioned why anyone would want to kill Abhishek and said a disturbance was bound to follow if a public space was occupied for a celebration.Union minister Sukanta Majumdar also criticised the decision to hold the gathering on a footpath. He said there was no objection to celebrating a birthday but argued that it should have been organised inside a residence or at a venue rather than on a public road.“If you block public roads in front of your house and hold a birthday celebration on the footpath, naturally people will get angry. The public is already upset with you; on top of that, if you behave like this, confrontations are bound to happen,” he said.Majumdar rejected allegations of BJP involvement and said the party did not want to “dirty its hands with small fry”.BJP leader Ritabrata Bandopadhyay also disputed the TMC’s account. He claimed local residents were angry because the gathering had obstructed roads used for transporting idols ahead of Kali Puja. He said the birthday celebration should have been held inside Abhishek’s residence.TMC MP Sougata Roy accused BJP workers of conducting a prior reconnaissance of the area before attacking Abhishek’s residence. He alleged that police personnel were present but failed to control the situation, and that some officers were also assaulted.Roy described the incident as an attempt to intimidate people and suppress the opposition.TMC MP Kirti Azad alleged that men armed with stones and sticks attacked the premises for 30 to 45 minutes. He claimed CCTV footage was available and accused the police of escorting those involved instead of arresting them.TMC MLA Kunal Ghosh also alleged that party workers were being targeted and questioned the police action following the incident. Party spokesperson and advocate Arka Nag described the episode as an alleged attempt to murder Abhishek and his supporters. He said the party had lodged a police complaint and questioned the imposition of prohibitory restrictions, arguing that they could affect the movement of Kali idols during the festival.The incident also drew reactions from leaders outside the two parties. Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury said nobody should be denied the right to celebrate a birthday. Congress leader Udit Raj described the incident as an unconstitutional act and an attack on democracy.Rashtriya Janata Dal MP Sudhakar Singh demanded President’s Rule in West Bengal, alleging that the state government had failed to maintain law and order.The confrontation comes against the backdrop of the BJP’s victory in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, which ended the TMC’s 15-year rule. The BJP is now in government, while the TMC, led by former chief minister Mamata Banerjee, is in opposition.The two parties have since traded allegations of violence and intimidation. The latest clash in Kalighat has added to the political tension in the state, with both sides blaming the other for the confrontation.With Kali Puja and Diwali approaching, the incident has also brought the arrangements for celebrations in Kalighat into the political dispute. Further details of the investigation and action against those detained are awaited.
Article Summary: Mamata Banerjee accuses the BJP of hooliganism and alleged a breakdown of law and order in the state. She said she had written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over the incident. The protest followed an overnight confrontation outside Abhishek’s residence.

Article Title: When the smoke settles, what remains? The unseen health and environmental risks
Article Text:
The science of festive pollution and its impact on our everyday lives. (Representative AI image)

Festive celebrations leave behind plastic waste, chemical residues and firecracker debris, polluting our air, water and soil.

Diwali and the science of air pollution

PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs, trigger inflammation and pose respiratory and cardiovascular health risks.

Beyond the lungs: How festive pollution affects multiple organs

Festive activities release a mix of chemicals, particulate matter and plastic waste, polluting air, water and soil.

Can a few hours of festive pollution cause lasting health problems?

Festive pollutants spread through air, water and soil, entering the food chain and threatening human health and ecosystems.

The environmental footprint of celebrations

Noise pollution: The impact beyond what we can see

The hidden burden of electricity consumption and festive shopping

Festive noise from firecrackers and loud music can damage hearing, disrupt sleep, trigger stress and affect heart health.

Why the effects can last beyond the festivities

Can celebrations become more environmentally responsible?

NEW DELHI: Festivals in India bring people together through lights, colours, music, food and community celebrations. From bursting firecrackers and decorating homes to playing with colours, organising processions and gathering along riverbanks, festivities are an integral part of the country's social and cultural life. But as celebrations grow in scale, so does their environmental footprint.The pollution generated during festivals is often discussed in isolation, particularly when air quality deteriorates after Diwali. However, the environmental impact of celebrations goes much further. Firecrackers release particulate matter into the atmosphere, synthetic colours can introduce chemicals into water bodies, large gatherings generate plastic waste, and loud music and fireworks contribute to noise pollution.These effects are not confined to a particular festival or community. Across different celebrations, the use of disposable materials, increased consumption, transportation, decorative lighting and improper waste disposal can put additional pressure on the environment.The consequences can extend beyond the days of festivities, affecting public health, urban sanitation, water quality and local ecosystems.In cities already struggling with vehicle emissions, industrial pollution, construction dust and untreated waste, the additional burden can make environmental management more challenging.So, what happens to the environment when millions of people celebrate simultaneously, and how do these activities affect our everyday lives?Diwali is among the occasions when the relationship between celebrations and air pollution becomes particularly visible. Firecrackers release a mixture of gases, suspended particles and chemical compounds into the atmosphere. Their emissions include particulate matter such as PM2.5 and PM10, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Depending on their composition, fireworks can also release metallic compounds, including barium and aluminium.The concern is particularly around PM2.5, particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less. These particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the bloodstream. Some components of particulate pollution can also enter the bloodstream and trigger inflammation.Dr Abhishek Agrawal, Medical Officer at a government hospital, explains how exposure to firecracker emissions can affect respiratory health."During festivals like Diwali, the concentration of pollutants in the air can increase due to firecracker emissions. People inhale these pollutants, particularly fine particulate matter, which can enter deep into the lungs and cause irritation and inflammation of the respiratory tract. We often see people complaining of coughing, throat irritation, breathlessness and worsening respiratory symptoms during periods of poor air quality. "The impact is not uniform across the population. Children, elderly people and individuals with pre-existing respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable to sudden changes in air quality."Children, elderly people and individuals suffering from asthma, COPD or other respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable. Their respiratory systems may not be able to cope with sudden exposure to high levels of pollution. Even people who do not have a pre-existing respiratory illness can experience discomfort, especially when pollution levels remain elevated for several hours," Agrawal said.The problem can also continue after the celebrations end. During the post-monsoon period, low wind speeds, atmospheric stability and temperature inversions can prevent pollutants from dispersing quickly. When firecracker emissions combine with existing sources such as vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions and construction dust, pollution levels can remain elevated."The effects of pollution do not necessarily disappear once the firecrackers stop. Fine particles can remain suspended in the atmosphere, depending on weather conditions. People may continue experiencing coughing, throat irritation, wheezing and breathing difficulties in the following days. Those with existing respiratory conditions should be especially cautious," Agrawal added.Air pollution is not merely a respiratory concern. Exposure to particulate matter, chemical emissions and excessive noise can affect several organs, including the heart, brain and nervous system.While the lungs are the first point of contact for inhaled pollutants, fine particles can trigger inflammatory responses that affect other parts of the body. Air pollution has been associated with increased blood pressure, disturbances in heart rhythm and a higher risk of cardiovascular complications, particularly among people with existing heart conditions."The impact of festive pollution is not limited to the lungs. Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, can penetrate deep into the alveoli and trigger oxidative stress and inflammation. This can lead to coughing, wheezing, breathlessness and asthma attacks. Air pollution can also increase blood pressure, disturb heart rhythms and trigger cardiovascular complications, including heart attacks, in vulnerable individuals," Agrawal explained.The brain and nervous system can also be affected. Exposure to polluted air and excessive noise can contribute to headaches, dizziness, stress and sleep disturbances. Prolonged exposure to air pollution has also been associated with adverse effects on cognitive health.Chemical exposure presents another concern. Certain toxic metals and chemical residues released by fireworks and other festive materials can pose risks to organs such as the kidneys and liver, depending on the substance, concentration and duration of exposure.Noise pollution adds another dimension to the health burden. Sudden, high-intensity sounds from firecrackers can cause tinnitus, temporary hearing discomfort and, at sufficiently high exposure levels, permanent hearing damage.One of the common misconceptions about festive pollution is that its effects are limited to the duration of celebrations. However, even short-term exposure to high concentrations of pollutants can trigger health complications, particularly among vulnerable individuals.People with asthma may experience sudden attacks, while those with existing respiratory or cardiovascular conditions may develop breathing difficulties or other complications. Repeated exposure over time can increase the risk of chronic health problems."Even a few hours of exposure to high levels of pollution can trigger asthma attacks, breathing difficulties and cardiovascular complications in vulnerable individuals. Repeated exposure increases the risk of long-term health problems. The duration of symptoms varies depending on the level of exposure and the person's health. Some people may recover within a few hours, while others may continue experiencing symptoms for several days," Agrawal said.The effects can also be reflected in healthcare demand. Indian studies examining air pollution during and after Diwali have reported increases in respiratory complaints, hospital visits and admissions, particularly involving asthma exacerbations and breathing difficulties."Studies in India have reported an increase in respiratory hospital visits and admissions following Diwali, particularly involving asthma attacks, breathing difficulties and other respiratory complaints. Hospitals and healthcare facilities also deal with cases involving burns, eye injuries and hearing-related problems during festive periods," Agrawal said.While air pollution receives considerable attention, other forms of environmental degradation often go unnoticed during festivals.The use of synthetic colours during celebrations, for instance, can create problems for water bodies and soil. Some commercially available colours may contain chemical compounds and heavy metals that can cause skin irritation, allergic reactions and eye problems. When washed away, these substances can enter drainage systems and eventually reach rivers, lakes and other water bodies.Similarly, religious offerings, flowers, plastic packaging and decorative materials discarded during large gatherings can add to water and land pollution. Idol immersion activities involving plaster of Paris, synthetic paints and non-biodegradable decorations can further increase the waste entering lakes and rivers.The consequences are particularly concerning in urban areas where water bodies are already under pressure from untreated sewage, industrial discharge and solid waste. Additional festive waste can worsen existing contamination and affect aquatic ecosystems.Large public celebrations and processions also generate considerable quantities of disposable plates, plastic bottles, food packaging and other materials. When waste is not segregated or collected properly, it can clog drains, accumulate in public spaces and eventually enter nearby water bodies.The problem does not end with the celebrations. Municipal sanitation workers are often left to clear large quantities of discarded materials, firecracker remnants, food waste and plastic packaging. Improper disposal and open burning of collected waste can further contribute to local pollution.Another dimension of festive pollution is noise, which can affect people even when there is no visible deterioration in air quality.Firecrackers, loudspeakers, musical processions and public celebrations can expose residential neighbourhoods to excessive sound levels. Sudden explosions and prolonged exposure to loud music can interfere with sleep, concentration and everyday routines.Repeated exposure to excessive noise can also contribute to stress, anxiety and hearing-related problems. People with cardiovascular conditions, infants, elderly residents and patients recovering from illnesses may be particularly affected by disturbances during late-night celebrations.The impact extends to animals and urban wildlife. Pets can experience distress due to sudden loud noises, while birds and other species may alter their movement and behaviour in response to repeated disturbances.The World Health Organization has associated excessive environmental noise with sleep disturbance, hearing impairment and cardiovascular health risks. This makes noise pollution an important public health concern rather than merely an inconvenience during celebrations.Modern celebrations also involve a considerable increase in consumption. Decorative lighting across homes, markets and commercial establishments increases electricity demand, while shopping, gift packaging, food deliveries and travel add to energy use and waste generation.Although LED lights consume less electricity than conventional lighting, their widespread use across residential and commercial areas can still contribute to higher cumulative demand.Excessive artificial lighting also contributes to light pollution, which can interfere with the natural day-night cycles of birds, insects and other wildlife. For nocturnal species, artificial illumination can affect navigation, feeding and other behavioural patterns.The growing use of plastic decorations, disposable utensils, thermocol, synthetic materials and packaging creates another challenge. Much of this waste is used for a limited period before being discarded, adding to the burden on already stretched municipal waste-management systems.These individual activities may appear relatively small, but their combined impact across densely populated cities can be considerable.One of the reasons festive pollution becomes a concern is that the environmental impact does not always end when celebrations stop.Airborne particles can remain suspended depending on weather conditions, while chemical residues and improperly disposed materials can continue affecting soil and water quality. Waste accumulated in drainage systems can also create problems during subsequent rainfall.The extent of pollution depends on several factors, including the scale of celebrations, the materials used, local environmental conditions and the efficiency of waste collection and disposal.It is also important to distinguish between pollution generated during festivals and the wider pollution crisis. Festivals are not the sole reason behind deteriorating air or water quality. Instead, they can add concentrated emissions and waste to an environment already dealing with multiple sources of contamination.This cumulative impact also raises questions about environmental inequality. A person celebrating indoors may have limited exposure to pollution, while a street vendor, traffic policeman, delivery worker or sanitation worker may remain exposed for several hours. Similarly, children and people with existing health conditions may face greater health risks than others.Reducing festive pollution does not mean giving up celebrations. It requires greater awareness of how everyday choices during these occasions affect the environment.Using natural colours, opting for traditional clay idols, avoiding single-use plastics, segregating waste and ensuring that religious offerings are disposed of responsibly can help reduce the burden on water bodies and public spaces. Community celebrations, designated immersion facilities and better waste collection can also improve environmental management.Individual precautions are equally important, particularly during periods of poor air quality. Agrawal recommends avoiding areas with heavy firecracker smoke, limiting outdoor activities when pollution levels are high and taking measures to reduce indoor exposure."People should avoid unnecessary outdoor activities when air quality is poor, particularly during early morning and late evening hours if pollution levels are elevated. Patients with asthma should follow their prescribed medication and treatment plans. Children and elderly people should limit exposure to smoke and avoid areas where firecrackers are being burst."He also recommends wearing a well-fitted N95 mask when outdoor exposure to particulate pollution cannot be avoided, keeping windows closed during periods of heavy pollution and using HEPA air purifiers indoors, if available.Outdoor exercise should be avoided when pollution levels are high. Firecracker residues should be cleaned using damp methods rather than dry sweeping, which can resuspend particles in the air.People experiencing persistent breathlessness, wheezing or chest pain should seek medical attention rather than dismissing the symptoms as temporary festive discomfort.Ultimately, the environmental cost of celebrations cannot be measured only by the pollution recorded on a particular day. It must also account for the waste left behind, the pressure on natural resources and the health implications for people who continue to live and work in these surroundings.Festivals are an important part of India's cultural and social fabric. The challenge is to ensure that the joy of celebrations does not come at the cost of the air people breathe, the water they depend on and the environment they share.
Article Summary: Festive activities release a mix of chemicals, particulate matter and plastic waste. PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs, trigger inflammation and pose respiratory and cardiovascular health risks. Children, elderly people and individuals with pre-existing respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable to sudden changes in air quality.

Article Title: 'From India to Pakistan, everyone invited': Anant Singh on daughter's grand wedding
Article Text:
Singh said everyone who had shown affection towards his family was welcome, regardless of where they came from

NEW DELHI: Expelled JD(U) leader Anant Singh said invitations for his daughter's grand wedding are being sent to people across India and Pakistan, insisting that political differences have no place at family celebrations. He said he would invite leaders across party lines, including Former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar and RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav.Speaking about the wedding preparations, Singh said everyone who had shown affection towards his family was welcome, regardless of where they came from."Everyone who has shown us love will come. The public is like God to us; whoever comes from wherever will be a gift to me. We are sending invitation cards to everyone. I want all my friends, well-wishers and people associated with us to attend. Everyone is invited. We are contacting everyone whose phone numbers we have. Not just Bihar, invitations are being sent across India and Pakistan. Are the invitations meant only for people in Bihar? They are for everyone, everywhere. We will invite everyone. There is no ruling party or Opposition at a wedding. Such divisions exist during elections and when seeking votes, but not at weddings and family celebrations.Yes, we will invite everyone, including Nitish Kumar and Lalu Prasad Yadav," he said.The wedding comes amid a turbulent political phase for Singh, who was expelled from the JD(U) along with his wife, former MLA Neelam Devi, for six years over alleged anti-party activities in October.The party's Bihar unit president Umesh Singh Kushwaha had announced the decision, accusing Singh of defying party directives, using insulting language against its top leadership and campaigning for a rival candidate in the recent legislative council elections.Despite being a JD(U) MLA, Singh had openly campaigned for Jan Suraaj Party candidate Anuj Singh against the party's nominee, MLC Neeraj Kumar, in the Patna Graduates' constituency election. The JD(U) also wrote to the Bihar Assembly Speaker seeking the termination of Singh's membership under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution. Neelam Devi's primary membership was also terminated over her alleged involvement in anti-party activities.The expulsion was followed by another setback for Singh in the Dularchand Yadav murder case. On October 30, he said he would comply with the Supreme Court's direction to surrender by December 1. The court issued the directive while hearing a plea seeking cancellation of the bail granted to him by the Patna High Court in March.Singh, who was arrested earlier in the case for allegedly orchestrating Yadav's murder in October last year, maintained that he had faith in the judiciary and expected to secure bail again after subsequent hearings.
Article Summary: Expelled JD(U) leader Anant Singh says political differences have no place at family celebrations. He said he would invite leaders across party lines, including Former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar and RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav. NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Friday said the results of the US midterm elections would have little impact on India-US relations, asserting that President Donald Trump retains considerable powers to pursue his foreign policy agenda despite the ruling party's electoral setback.Speaking in Thiruvananthapuram, Tharoor said the US election results would not change Washington's approach towards key issues such as tariffs, sanctions on countries buying Russian oil, the Iran war or the Ukraine conflict."Whether it comes to tariffs, whether it comes to sanctions for buying Russian oil, whether it comes to the Iran war itself, whether it comes to any initiative he takes on the Ukraine war. All of this, he's completely unaffected by the election result," Tharoor said.He explained that while Congress has significant powers over budgetary matters and can restrict or approve government spending, the President enjoys considerable discretion in foreign policy and international affairs.Tharoor said that even when it comes to military action, the President can proceed without seeking approval for an initial period of up to 60 days. However, Congress can exercise its financial powers to restrict expenditure, particularly in the case of an expensive military campaign."Those in India who are expecting this to have some impact on our relationship with the US, I think, are completely mistaken," he said.Commenting on the election outcome, Tharoor described it as an extraordinary setback for the ruling party, pointing out that midterm elections traditionally serve as a course correction for the party in power.He also highlighted the gains made by candidates from minority communities and people of Indian origin, including the election of a mayor of Indian origin in Los Angeles.Tharoor said the results reflected the vibrancy of American democracy but maintained that the outcome would not significantly alter Trump's ability to take decisions on international affairs.

Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The Union home ministry has relaxed passport and visa requirements for several categories of foreign nationals residing in India, including Pakistani citizens who entered prior to December 31, 2009 with the intention to permanently reside in India but could not renew their Pakistani passport due to non-possession of computerised nationality identity card issued by Pakistan government.Other categories of foreign nationals for whom passport and visa rules have been eased as part of the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) (Amendment) ORder, 2026, include citizens of Pakistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan belonging to their religious minorities; Sri Lankan Tamil refugees and Tibetans.The order also streamlines travel and identification protocols for the citizens of Nepal and Bhutan, allowing them to enter or exit India by producing any one of the documents specified in the visa manual; However, in case they are entering or exiting India from or to a place other than Nepal or Bhutan, they must in possession of a valid passport. Nepal and Bhutan citizens who have embarked at or transited through China Macau, Hong Kong or Pakistan, must be in possession of both a valid passport and valid visa.The requirement of a valid passport and visa would also not apply to a male member of the Muslim community, being originally an Indian citizen, who went to Pakistan after partition between August 15, 1947 and Dec 31, 1965 leaving behind family in India and returned to India on or before Dec 31, 2009, and settled in Keralam on a valid Pakistani passport but which has since expired or been lost.However, such a person should not have married or acquired immoveable property while in Pakistan; ,while going to Pakistan, left behind family members who are Indian citizens; shall not return to Pakistan; and should not have any adverse report from the police or security agencies.A citizen of India entering into India from Nepal or Bhutan or departing from India to Nepal or Bhutan by land or air shall produce before the immigration officer one of the documents specified in the visa manual to establish their identity, though this exemption would not be applicable if departing to or returning from countries other than Nepal or Bhutan through the Indo-Nepal or Indo-Bhutan border of by air. In all such cases, a valid passport will be required and the exit and entry into India shall be only through the designated immigration points.The provisions in the Act and rules with regard to requirement of valid passport or other valid travel document and valid visa for entry into, stay in and exit from India, shall also not apply for a member of naval, military or air forces of India, entering into or exiting from India on duty and members of the family of any such person when accompanying him on a government transport; registered Sri Lankan Tamil nationals who have taken shelter in India up to Jan 9, 2015; as well as the foreign crew of foreign military vessels coming for repairs in India who are granted military ship repair permits by the immigration officer, provided they hold their military identification documents.Exempted categories include a Tibetan who has entered India after 1959 but before May 30,, 2003 on an entry permit issued by the Embassy of India in Kathmandu; or who entered after May 30, 2003, on the special entry permit issued through the designated immigration post on the Indo-Nepal border and a certificate of registration was issued by the registration officer concerned.Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Christian, Jain and Parsi citizens of Pakistan who entered India before Dec 31, 2024, fearing religious persecution in their home country, without valid documents including passport or other travel documents; or with valid documents including passport that has since expired, would also get relief under the amended Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) order. However, such a person shall be required to obtain an appropriate category of visa after their entry into India, for continued stay.Also exempt now from requirement of a valid passport and visa are persons of Indian origin who subsequently acquired the citizenship of Malaysia or Singapore and returned to India on or before Dec 31, 2009 on a valid passport issued by either of those countries, which has since expired and is not being renewed by those countries because such person does not meet the conditions specified by those countries. Such persons must have documentary proof that they are a person of Indian origin.
Article Summary: The order also streamlines travel and identification protocols for the citizens of Nepal and Bhutan. Pakistani citizens who entered prior to December 31, 2009 could not renew their Pakistani passport due to non-possession of computerised nationality identity card. Other categories of foreign nationals for whom passport and visa rules have been eased include citizens of Pakistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan belonging to their religious minorities.

NEW DELHI: Contributions received by the Congress in excess of Rs 20,000 totalled Rs 130.7 crore in 2025-26, which is barely one-fourth of its Rs 517.4 crore donation receipts in 2024-25.As per the 2025-26 contribution report of the Congress filed with EC, Prudent Electoral Trust contributed 19% of Congress's total donation kitty in the relevant year. In 2024-25, Prudent had accounted for 41.8% of contributions received by Congress.Prudent is the only electoral trust through which donations, largely corporate, were routed to Congress last year. At Rs 25 crore, the trust's contributions to the party, however, were only 11.5% of the Rs 216 crore funds it had channelled to the party in 2024-25.The steep 75% decline in Congress's total contributions in excess of Rs 20,000, compared with 2024-25, could be due to several factors. Given that 2024-25 was the general election year, a marked rise (84% as compared to 2023-24) in contributions to the main opposition party was on expected lines. What is interesting though is that the Rs 130.7 crore contribution receipts in 2025-26 are nearly 53% less than the amount it had received even in 2023-24.The steep decline was witnessed despite 2025-26 being the year of Bihar assembly elections and the run-up to elections in Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Puducherry held in April 2026.The Congress audit report for 2025-26, which is not available yet, will throw light on the party's other sources of funding. In 2024-25, Congress's collection from the issuance and sale of coupons was over Rs 350 crore.Among the key contributors last year, other than Prudent, were Star Cement Ltd (Rs 5 crore), Sajjan Bhajanka (Rs 4 crore), Afnan Constructions (Rs 3 crore), Prem Kumar Bhajanka (Rs 2 crore) and IPSUM Proadvisors and SMS Builders (Rs 1 crore each).Just nine contributions of Rs 1 crore or more accounted for Rs 43 crore, or nearly one-third of the party's total receipts. In comparison, 1,321 contributions of Rs 5 lakh or less together added up to Rs 37.2 crore, accounting for just 28.5% of the total. The median contribution among the 1,735 entries was Rs 3 lakh, highlighting how a relatively small number of large donations accounted for a substantial share of the party's funding.
Article Summary: contributions received by the Congress in excess of Rs 20,000 totalled Rs 130.7 crore in 2025-26. This is barely one-fourth of its Rs 517.4 crore donation receipts in 2024-25. Just nine contributions of Rs 1 crore or more accounted for Rs 43 crore.

How the Emergency divided the Gandhi family

Sonia recalls Babri mosque demolition

NEW DELHI: Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi has described the imposition of the Emergency as a mistake, saying she believes her mother-in-law and then prime minister Indira Gandhi eventually came to regret the decision.The Congress leader in her upcoming book "Belonging: A Journey of Love" also writes that keeping Sanjay Gandhi "in check" could have prevented much of the damage that followed the imposition of the Emergency, according to her interview with The Guardian ahead of the book’s release."I always feel that Mrs (Indira) Gandhi was a democrat at heart," Sonia told the British daily. "I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her," she added.According to The Guardian, Sonia recalled that the decision to impose the Emergency divided the family.Her husband, Rajiv Gandhi , had reportedly advised his mother to wait until the next election, while Sanjay argued that the opposition would destroy her and had to be stopped.Sonia said the disagreement also created tensions within the family, as Rajiv tried to confront his mother but she refused to listen."Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed," she wrote in the book, according to The Guardian.In a separate interview with The Hindu, published on Saturday, Sonia said Sanjay was not the only person who influenced the decision.She pointed to pressure from some of Indira's senior colleagues and said few people around the then prime minister shared Rajiv's views."It was not only Sanjay, though in the public mind he is often seen as synonymous with the Emergency. There was a lot of pressure from some of her senior colleagues, and I think there were very few people around her like Rajiv who had a different point of view," she said."I think eventually my mother-in-law began to understand the situation through her own wisdom and took actions to remedy it," she added.Sonia said she became aware of the full gravity of the events only after the Emergency ended. While acknowledging that democratic rights had been curtailed and habeas corpus suspended, she said the measures had been taken constitutionally."It was only after the Emergency that I came to know the true gravity of what had been happening. Yes, democratic rights had been curtailed and there was a suspension of habeas corpus, but it was done constitutionally," she said.Looking back, Sonia said Indira had been struggling to deal with the deteriorating situation at the time."Yet, when I take myself back to that period and try and see it from Mrs Indira Gandhi's point of view, I see her struggling to cope with the rapidly deteriorating prevailing circumstances: violent protests, government offices and public transport set on fire, widespread organised unrest and even a call for the bureaucracy and armed forces to disobey orders," she said.Sonia said hindsight helped put the events into perspective. She also pointed out that Indira later called elections and publicly expressed regret over the excesses committed during the Emergency."And you know very well that she herself later publicly expressed regret and apologised for excesses during the Emergency," she said.In her interview with The Guardian, Sonia also recalled crying as she watched the Babri mosque being demolished in December 1992.She said the incident made her realise that the country faced "a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build", the British daily reported.Sonia also acknowledged that the Congress had, in part, contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics."I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude," she said.Indira Gandhi imposed the Emergency shortly before midnight on June 25, 1975. President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued the proclamation on her recommendation, and the Union Cabinet later ratified it.On January 18, 1977, Indira announced fresh Lok Sabha elections and released political prisoners. She and Sanjay Gandhi were defeated in the March 1977 elections. The Emergency officially ended on March 21, 1977.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi says keeping Sanjay Gandhi "in check" could have prevented much of the damage that followed the imposition of the Emergency. Sonia says she became aware of the full gravity of the events only after the Emergency ended. Sonia also recalled crying as she watched the Babri mosque being demolished in December 1992. NEW DELHI: Postgraduate doctors are walking away from residency programmes at some of India's leading medical institutions. RTI replies show exits across AIIMS campuses and JIPMER , with AIIMS Delhi alone reporting 34 junior resident departures in 2025.While several institutes lack consolidated data on psychiatric counselling or workplace stress among residents, Dr Lakshya Mittal, chairperson of United Doctors Front (UDF), said multiple RTI applications filed by its members had revealed postgraduate doctors quitting premier medical institutions despite securing top NEET-PG ranks. He cited complaints of duties extending beyond 36 hours, workplace harassment, toxic work culture and inadequate support.“Residency is meant to train doctors, not break them. Discipline is not humiliation and dedication is not exploitation,” Mittal said, urging authorities to enforce working-hour regulations, establish independent grievance-redressal mechanisms and fix institutional accountability. UDF has also filed a PIL in the Supreme Court.However, the figures from individual institutions show that departures have continued, even as some reported a decline.At AIIMS Delhi, 34 junior resident doctors quit in 2025, compared with 60 in 2024, a decline of about 43%. The number of residents joining also fell, from 324 in 2024 to 267 in 2025. Department-wise figures show the highest number of exits in anaesthesiology at seven, followed by ophthalmology at six. Surgery reported three exits, as did pathology. Ophthalmology had recorded 14 exits in 2024.JIPMER, Puducherry, also reported a decline in resignations. A combined count of departures from its January and July batches shows 44 residents resigned in 2025, compared with 60 in 2024, a fall of nearly 27%. However, exits continued across several specialities, including anaesthesiology, emergency medicine, orthopaedics, pathology and surgery.The trend is not confined to these two institutions. AIIMS Kalyani reported 15 exits across all three years of postgraduate training in 2025, including 13 from the January and July batches. Another 11 students from the 2026 batches had left by the time of its reply. AIIMS Raipur reported 19 exits from its 2025 batches, AIIMS Patna 12, while AIIMS Gorakhpur also reported departures. At AIIMS Rishikesh, 30 students across various postgraduate and super-speciality programmes left in 2025.The RTI also sought details of psychiatric counselling and whether stress, depression or sleep deprivation were recorded as reasons for leaving. AIIMS Delhi said it had no compiled counselling data, while AIIMS Rishikesh reported six postgraduate students receiving psychiatric counselling in 2026 but maintained no consolidated record of workplace-related stress. AIIMS Raipur reported no residents seeking counselling in 2025 or 2026.AIIMS Patna reported 15 residents receiving counselling in 2025 and none in 2026, while AIIMS Kalyani declined to provide the information, citing RTI provisions.The figures are not directly comparable as institutes provided data for different periods and batches. While they establish that residents are leaving, the reasons remain unclear, with several institutes lacking records that could help explain the departures.
Article Summary: Postgraduate doctors are walking away from residency programmes at some of India's leading medical institutions. RTI replies show exits across AIIMS campuses and JIPMER. At AIIMs Delhi, 34 junior resident doctors quit in 2025, compared with 60 in 2024, a decline of about 43%.

Gandhi grip amid Congress losses

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi appeared to sidestep questions about the Gandhi family's continued control of the party and allegations of nepotism during an interview with British newspaper The Guardian, saying the question of its leadership should be put to the party itself.“You would have to ask the party,” she told the interviewer when asked why the Congress had not moved beyond the Gandhi family's leadership.The newspaper said Sonia Gandhi “skates over the question of nepotism”, quoting her response to the charge that the party is controlled by one family. “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have,” Sonia Gandhi said in a vague answer to nepotism charge.The interview was published on Saturday, alongside an edited extract from her memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love", which is due to be released early next week.Sonia maintained that the Congress could still emerge as a credible alternative to the BJP. However, the interviewer noted that many people remained unconvinced after the party's repeated electoral defeats.The article pointed to the Congress's decline under Rahul Gandhi's leadership. After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The party is now in power in only a few states, while the BJP's Hindutva ideology has become the country's dominant political force.The newspaper observed that the Gandhi family's continued control had made it difficult for the Congress to shake off allegations of nepotism and leadership by political elites.Sonia was also defensive when asked about the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, which remained in power for a decade until 2014, and the controversies surrounding its tenure.“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” she said, responding to the criticism.The conversation also turned to the Emergency imposed by her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi , in 1975.She described the decision as a “mistake” and said she believed Indira herself eventually came to feel the same way.“I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her,” the ex-Congress president said.Sonia said the Gandhi family was “split on the decision” to impose the Emergency.According to the newspaper's account, her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, opposed the move and advised his mother to wait for the next election. Her younger son, Sanjay Gandhi, reportedly pushed for a tougher response to the Opposition.At a family dinner, Sanjay is said to have warned Indira that the Opposition would destroy her, telling her, “They must be stopped”. His influence over his mother became a major source of public controversy.Sonia recalled that the decision “inflamed tensions” within the family. Rajiv reportedly tried to confront his mother, but she refused to listen.“Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” it quoted from her book.Sonia also spoke about the personal trauma of losing her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, who was assassinated in 1991. She struggled to recall how she carried on after his death, with her daughter Priyanka also joining the conversation at her residence.She recalled the assassination of Indira Gandhi in 1984, when she heard what sounded like fireworks before seeing her mother-in-law's body covered in blood and bullet wounds. Indira had been shot by two of her bodyguards.Sonia described trying to revive her as they rushed her to hospital.“There was blood everywhere, and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she remembered.She described the journey to the hospital as “excruciating”. Despite the relatively light traffic, the drive seemed painfully slow. She said she knew Indira might already be dead because she was no longer responding.Sonia also recalled the trauma and depression that followed, saying she lived “like a ghost”. The conversation touched on Rajiv's private expression of grief during that difficult period.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi appeared to sidestep questions about the Gandhi family's continued control of the party. She said the question of its leadership should be put to the party itself. The interview was published on Saturday, alongside an edited extract from her memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love", due to be released early next week.

Article Title: A century for Bharat Ratna Advani!
Article Text:

"As a voter of Gandhinagar, I also had the honour of voting for Advani Ji on numerous occasions."

"Advani Ji was a fiery Opposition leader but an equally excellent administrator."
