Shri Lal Krishna Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life today, 8th November. This year, his birthday fittingly coincides with Diwali , a festival associated with Prabhu Shri Ram and the Diya at a time when we are marking 75 years since the inception of the Jana Sangh, 125th Jayanti of Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee and recently celebrated a hundred years of the RSS There are very few people whose lives have touched so many different chapters of modern India. Advani Ji was born on 8th November 1927, on Dev Deepawali. As a youngster in 1947, he experienced the pain of leaving behind his familiar world in Sindh. He rebuilt his life from scratch without bitterness. This trait of being able to build from scratch, against all odds, has stayed with him throughout. It was seen while he was strengthening the Jana Sangh and later building the BJP. His tenures as BJP President saw the Congress falling sharply from 400 to below 200 in 1989 and the BJP becoming the single largest party for the first time in 1996. Advani Ji nurtured generations of Karyakartas and gave the Party a clear foundation rooted in the principle of Nation First.Two qualities always set Advani Ji apart as a leader. First, his ideological clarity and intellectual sharpness. This was reflected in his speeches and writings.The Jana Sangh and BJP resolutions he authored remain worth reading even today, while his interviews were consistently incisive and precise. Second, the manner in which he exposed the pseudo-secularism propounded by a large section of the Indian polity for many years.Advani Ji took up every responsibility with immense diligence. As an RSS Pracharak, Advani Ji first worked in different parts of Rajasthan. From there, he went to the national capital, where he started working closely with Atal Ji. History shows that it is rare for two towering political leaders to work together for several decades, cooperating with each other without becoming competitors. Advani Ji and Atal Ji set a remarkable example. Together, they changed the course of Indian politics.The Delhi that Advani Ji came to was coming to terms with the horrors of Partition. He immersed himself in making the Jana Sangh stronger. In 1967, Advani Ji became the Chairman of the Delhi Metropolitan Council, where he worked alongside the late Vijay Kumar Malhotra Ji (who became Chief Executive Councillor).In 1970, Advani Ji’s Parliamentary innings began. His interventions have won appreciation across the political spectrum. He made a mark as an MP and later, as Leader of Opposition in both houses and from the treasury benches too. Despite parliamentary commitments, he frequently travelled across India meeting people.I vividly recall the 1991 Lok Sabha elections. It was decided that Advani Ji would contest the Lok Sabha elections from two seats, one of which was Gandhinagar. He had an old link with Gujarat. His father had settled in Kutch after Partition. Advani Ji had also served as a Rajya Sabha MP from Gujarat. So, it was a homecoming of sorts. Being involved in the BJP organisation, I had the honour of helping prepare his papers and assisting him throughout the campaign. The people of Gandhinagar sent him to Parliament time and again. As a voter of Gandhinagar, I also had the honour of voting for Advani Ji on numerous occasions. The care and attention he devoted to his constituency is something to learn from.The Emergency was a watershed moment in Advani Ji’s life. He was at the forefront of saving democracy and protecting the Constitution. His experiences found their way into his book, ‘A Prisoner's Scrap-Book.’ One part of that book, titled ‘A Tale of Two Emergencies’, beautifully explained the striking similarities between the events in India starting June 1975 and those in Nazi Germany in 1933.Advani Ji was a fiery Opposition leader but an equally excellent administrator. When the Janata Government came to office in 1977, Advani Ji became Minister for Information and Broadcasting. It is widely accepted that his work in this department was extremely impactful. As Deputy Prime Minister and one of India’s longest-serving Home Ministers, he was instrumental in strengthening India’s security apparatus. His work in improving the lives of our security forces is remembered with great fondness. His unequivocal stand against terrorism ensured India got a tough anti-terror law.Of course, an iconic moment in Advani Ji’s life was the Somnath to Ayodhya Rath Yatra. It changed the course of Indian society for the better. I consider it a privilege that I got the opportunity to be involved in this Yatra from the ideation stage to execution. Being present at Somnath when the Yatra began was particularly special. A Yatra can be very demanding, requiring long hours, constant travel, physical endurance and an ability to remain focused despite fatigue. Advani Ji embodied this endurance.I also have memories of the saddening moments of Advani Ji’s arrest in Bihar. Then, in Gujarat, the BJP withdrew support from the Chimanbhai Patel Government. With this, a simple message was given, that when it comes to our ideology and the Ram Temple, there will never be any compromise. Many of our senior leaders and Karyakartas took an oath that, come what may, a Ram Temple will be built. And, years later, with the blessings of the people of India, a grand Mandir for Prabhu Shri Ram became a reality in Ayodhya.There is so much more of Advani Ji that is outstanding. His simplicity, for example. After the Navnirman Movement, Advani Ji had come to Junagadh and stayed for a month as an ordinary Karyakarta, preparing the Party for the Assembly elections in which Congress was rejected. He has always shown what probity in public life is about. He is a voracious reader. Those who have spent time with him know how carefully he goes through newspapers. He is a big fan of cinema and theatre, and has been an enthusiastic film critic. His sense of history and the need to preserve it is visible in his book, ‘My Country My Life.’Advani Ji always remained in touch with Sindhi culture. Another effort he undertook was the popularisation of Sindhu Darshan Puja near Leh. I myself had been to one Puja with Advani Ji and George Fernandes Ji.Any account of Advani Ji’s remarkable journey would be incomplete without mentioning Kamla Advani Ji. She was a constant source of strength and support throughout his public life.Growing up in Karachi, Advani Ji could hardly have imagined the path his life would take. In an expression of gratitude, the people of India conferred upon him the Bharat Ratna in 2024. As Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life, I pray that he be blessed with good health and that he continues to inspire us all as he has always done.
Article Summary: Advani Ji was born on 8th November 1927, on Dev Deepawali. This year, his birthday fittingly coincides with Diwali, a festival associated with Prabhu Shri Ram and the Diya. His tenures as BJP President saw the Congress falling sharply from 400 to below 200 in 1989.

Article Title: Digital arrest: A cyberfraud wrapped in a psychological trap; why intelligence falls prey to basic instincts
Article Text:
A government report describes cybercrime in India as having evolved from a "distant threat into a pervasive everyday reality".

No legal basis for digital arrest

The magnitude of digital arrests

More than digital, it's psychological

India's fight against digital arrests

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Last week, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant expressed exasperation over the growing number of "digital arrest" scams, questioning how even educated people continued to fall victim to them despite repeated public awareness campaigns."What is wrong with these victims? How are these victims being trapped like this? They can't understand this basic thing? What's the fear of arrest on mobile?" the CJI orally observed while hearing a suo motu case on digital arrests."Hit the mobile on the wall and arrest goes. Something is wrong with people. God knows what is there. What kind of person are you in a democratic country if you think you are getting arrested on mobile?" he added.But is it really that simple?Every day, people across the country fall victim to these scams. It often begins with an unfamiliar voice on the phone, claiming that the person has been implicated in a crime. What follows is a carefully orchestrated web of threats, intimidation and psychological manipulation, with victims drawn deeper into the trap over phone and video calls.As society evolves, so does crime. While traditional theft involved breaking into homes, cracking safes or carrying out armed robberies, the expansion of digital technology has opened up new avenues for criminals.Increasingly, fraudsters no longer need to come face to face with their victims to rob them.Digital arrest is one such sophisticated form of cyber fraud . Criminals impersonate police officers or officials of investigative agencies, convincing unsuspecting people that they are under investigation for serious offences.Typically, the scam begins with a phone or video call in which fraudsters claim that the victim's identity has been linked to crimes such as money laundering, drug trafficking or other illegal activities.Victims are then made to believe that they are under constant surveillance and instructed to remain on video calls for hours, sometimes even days, without contacting family members or anyone else. To lend credibility to their claims, scammers often produce forged arrest warrants, court orders and official-looking identity documents, making the threat of legal action appear genuine.The intimidation eventually gives way to demands for money. Victims are instructed to transfer funds to designated bank accounts for supposed verification, security clearance or to avoid arrest.But digital arrest has no legal basis. No law enforcement agency can arrest someone over a video call or demand money to prevent prosecution. Nor do authorities issue or serve arrest warrants through video calls, WhatsApp, emails or other messaging platforms.The scale of the problem is reflected in government data. According to a 2025 response in the Rajya Sabha, reported digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes in India nearly tripled between 2022 and 2024, while the amount defrauded increased more than 21-fold.Replying to a parliamentary question, minister of state for home affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar furnished data on digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes reported on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (NCRP) over the three-year period.The data showed that 39,925 incidents were reported in 2022, involving a total defrauded amount of Rs 91.14 crore. By 2024, the number of reported incidents had risen to 1,23,672, while the amount defrauded had surged to Rs 1,935.51 crore.The growing sophistication and scale of these scams have also drawn the attention of the Supreme Court.In October 2025, the court took suo motu cognizance of the issue after a senior citizen couple from Haryana approached it, alleging that fraudsters posing as investigative agency officials had cheated them of more than Rs 1 crore using forged court documents.Investigations have also brought into focus the organised networks operating behind these frauds, including syndicates based overseas. A major challenge for investigators is tracing the money trail, with criminals using intermediary or "mule" bank accounts to receive stolen funds and rapidly transfer them across multiple accounts to evade detection.The persistence of these scams raises an important question: Why do some people fall for something that may appear obviously fraudulent to others?Speaking to The Times of India, clinical psychologist Yukta Sharma said phishing and cyberfraud should not be dismissed as instances of poor judgement. Instead, they exploit ordinary human responses to fear, uncertainty, authority and the promise of rewards."Phishing is not merely a technological problem. The technology provides the medium, but the actual vulnerability being exploited is often human psychology," Sharma said, adding that even people who are intellectually well-equipped can fall prey to such traps.According to her, scammers deliberately create situations designed to provoke an immediate emotional response. This could be fear of losing money, anxiety over possible legal consequences, excitement about a potential reward or trust in someone posing as an authority figure."When an individual is being targeted through a phishing attempt, there is often a complex interplay of emotional arousal, cognitive processing and decision-making taking place. These attacks deliberately create situations that trigger an immediate emotional response, whether it is fear of losing money, anxiety about legal consequences, excitement over a potential reward or trust in an apparently legitimate authority," she said."Once these emotions are activated, the individual's attention tends to become increasingly focused on resolving the perceived situation rather than questioning its authenticity," Sharma told TOI.She explained that victims may move gradually from initial suspicion to compliance as fraudsters build credibility through convincing explanations, repeated instructions and sustained pressure.By the time the deception is exposed, victims are often left dealing with shock, disbelief, guilt, embarrassment and anxiety. The experience can be particularly distressing because they may struggle to understand how they were manipulated into surrendering their money.A NITI Aayog report describes cybercrime in India as having evolved from a "distant threat into a pervasive everyday reality". Recognising the growing challenge, the Centre has stepped up efforts to combat digital fraud and strengthen the country's cybercrime response.One of the key initiatives is the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), established by the ministry of home affairs to coordinate national efforts to tackle cybercrime and support its prevention and investigation.To address financial cyber fraud, the government launched the financial cyber fraud reporting system in 2021, enabling victims to report incidents quickly. According to the report, the system has helped save more than Rs 3,431 crore across 9.94 lakh complaints.The government has also strengthened cyber forensic capabilities through the National Cyber Forensic Laboratory in Delhi and the Evidence Lab in Hyderabad, enhancing the ability of law enforcement agencies to examine and analyse digital evidence.The I4C's online training platform, CyTrain, meanwhile, aims to equip police personnel and judicial officers with the skills required to investigate and prosecute cybercrime.The Reserve Bank of India is also exploring the possibility of introducing a 'kill switch' mechanism that would allow potential victims to immediately block all financial transactions from their accounts.But are these measures enough to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated cybercriminals?Former Bihar director general of police Abhayanand believes digital arrest scams must be treated as serious cases of organised cheating, requiring a specialised and professional police response.Speaking to TOI, he said cybercrime has traditionally been one of the weaker areas of policing, largely because perpetrators are difficult to trace and may operate across state or international borders."Digital arrest is a sophisticated form of cheating and the police must treat it as such. It is a combination of cybercrime and traditional fraud. Cybercrime has traditionally been one of the weak areas for the police, as it is often difficult to trace the source of the crime. The perpetrators could be operating from another state or even another country," the former DGP said."To tackle such cases effectively, the police need specialised training and must approach these investigations with professionalism," he added.Cyber and privacy law expert advocate Prashant Mali, meanwhile, argued that India needs stronger financial surveillance, more accountable telecom infrastructure and faster action against fraudulent accounts to tackle the menace."I feel we need stronger financial surveillance, accountable telecom infrastructure, faster freezing of fraudulent accounts, international cooperation and effective law enforcement," Mali told TOI.He also criticised the lack of effective deterrence against cybercriminals, arguing that convictions in cybercrime cases remain in single digits."I feel government is not able to create deterrence in the minds of cyber criminals engaged in the brutal digital arrest, cyber crime. We need to make an example of the crime digital arrest related convictions, but the convictions in cybercrime matters are in single figures," he said.Mali also proposed a government-backed insurance mechanism to protect victims of digital fraud, arguing that the financial burden should not fall on those who have already been cheated. "I feel government asked for digital India as the flagship program. Now digital arrest is the fallout where unsuspecting victims are falling prey to fraud. We need digital India insurance for digital arrest victims where the premium is paid by government and banking, financial services, and insurance participants and not by the victim. Every Indian should be secured from a digital accident like the digital arrest by Digital India Insurance," he suggested.As India pushes ahead with its digital transformation, cybercriminals are finding increasingly sophisticated ways to exploit the same technology. The fight against digital arrest scams, therefore, cannot rest on awareness campaigns or individual vigilance alone. It will require better-trained police forces, stronger financial safeguards, faster investigations and a system that can respond as swiftly as the fraudsters operate.The CJI's question about why people continue to fall for these scams is important. But the answer lies not simply in telling victims to be more careful. It lies in understanding how fear and manipulation can override rational judgement, and building institutions capable of protecting people when that happens.
Article Summary: Digital arrest is a sophisticated form of cyber fraud. Criminals impersonate police officers or officials of investigative agencies. They convince unsuspecting people that they are under investigation for serious offences. But digital arrest has no legal basis. No law enforcement agency can arrest someone over a video call.

CHENNAI: The Indian Medical Association (IMA) has asked the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) to refuse certification to the Hindi film Suryaa: Ant Se Aarambh Tak, starring Sunny Deol and Ravi Kishan, which is slated for release on Nov 20.The IMA objects to the film's teaser, released on Oct 19. In it, a father who has lost his daughter says doctors "write commission slips" instead of prescriptions, then asks how long people will tolerate this. The teaser then shows him assaulting doctors and nursing staff members inside a hospital, which the IMA says is presented as a heroic and justified act.In a representation dated Nov 4, IMA national president Dr Anilkumar J Nayak urged the board to deny certification under Section 4(2)(v) read with Section 5B(1) of the Cinematograph Act, 1952, and the 2026 certification guidelines.The association said the objectionable content is the film's core theme and cannot be removed by mere excisions.The IMA wants the board to refuse certification to any trailer, teaser or promotional material that shows violence against doctors, nurses or hospital staff, or carries dialogue imputing corruption to doctors as a class.It has sought a screening under Section 7C for IMA representatives, the presence of an IMA-nominated medical expert when the examining committee views the film, and a hearing before any decision is taken.It said if any certificate is recommended, the chairperson should refer the film to a revising committee under Rule 25(1) of the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024. It wants every scene showing violence against healthcare workers as justified or heroic deleted, along with the dialogue on corruption. It also wants a prominent disclaimer that the film does not represent the medical profession and that such violence is punishable.The association asked for a written, reasoned decision and priority consideration given the release date. It reserved the right to approach the courts.
Article Summary: The IMA objects to the film's teaser, released on Oct 19. In it, a father who has lost his daughter says doctors "write commission slips" instead of prescriptions. The teaser then shows him assaulting doctors and nursing staff members inside a hospital. The IMA says is presented as a heroic and justified act.

Article Title: Data protection law faces scrutiny: The key concerns explained
Article Text:
The legal challenge raises questions over how the law could affect investigative journalism, RTI access and government accountability

Parliament passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in August 2023.

What is the DPDP Act and why was it introduced?

What does the law provide?

The framework is responsible for examining complaints, conducting inquiries and determining penalties.

Why are news publishers challenging the law?

What do legal experts say about press freedom?

RTI amendment: Why is Section 44(3) under scrutiny?

The debate has produced differing assessments of whether journalism needs a separate exemption under the legislation.

Could government powers affect journalistic sources?

Is the Data Protection Board independent?

What has the government said?

When will the law come into effect fully?

What happens next?

The larger question: Can privacy and public interest coexist?

India's new data protection framework was introduced with a clear objective: to give citizens greater control over their personal information and make organisations accountable for how they collect, store and use it. But as the government moves towards implementing the law, a growing debate has emerged over whether safeguards designed to protect individual privacy could also affect investigative journalism, access to public records and government accountability.The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, is facing a legal challenge from the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents 21 news organisations. The association has approached the Supreme Court, arguing that several provisions of the law and its accompanying rules could restrict journalistic activities, compromise confidential sources and undermine the Right to Information (RTI) framework.The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on October 27 and listed the matter for further hearing on November 17. The government, meanwhile, has indicated that it is open to amending the rules or even the law itself if necessary to address concerns over press freedom.The challenge has brought an important question into focus: Where should the line be drawn between an individual's right to privacy and the public's right to know? While one view holds that constitutional protections and judicial scrutiny can address competing interests, another argues that journalism needs explicit statutory safeguards.Parliament passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in August 2023, establishing a legal framework to regulate the processing of digital personal information.The legislation came against the backdrop of India's rapidly expanding digital economy, where personal information has become central to everyday activities. Banking transactions, online shopping, digital payments, social media accounts, healthcare services and government welfare schemes all involve the collection and processing of personal data.While this has made services more accessible, it has also increased the risks of data breaches, identity theft, unauthorised sharing and misuse of personal information.The need for a comprehensive data protection framework gained importance after the Supreme Court, in its landmark 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, recognised privacy as a fundamental right under the Constitution.The DPDP Act seeks to establish obligations for organisations handling personal data and provide individuals with rights over how their information is processed.The ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, on November 14, 2025, following consultations with stakeholders.According to a Press Information Bureau (PIB) backgrounder published on November 17, 2025, the government received 6,915 inputs during the consultation process. These included suggestions from startups, micro, small and medium enterprises, industry bodies, civil society organisations, government departments and citizens.The government described the framework as citizen-centric, with an emphasis on consent, transparency, accountability and responsible use of digital personal information.The Act revolves around two key categories: Data Fiduciaries and Data Principals.A Data Fiduciary is an organisation or individual that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. This could include a bank collecting customer details, an e-commerce platform storing purchase histories or a company maintaining employee records.A Data Principal is the individual to whom the personal information belongs.The legislation requires Data Fiduciaries to obtain consent before processing personal data, except in specified circumstances where processing is permitted under the law. Such consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous.Individuals must also be informed about the purpose for which their information is being collected and how it will be used.The Act provides Data Principals with several rights, including the right to access information about the processing of their personal data, seek correction and erasure, withdraw consent and raise grievances. They can also nominate another person to exercise their rights in certain circumstances.Organisations are required to implement reasonable security safeguards to protect personal information. In case of a data breach, they must notify the Data Protection Board of India and affected individuals in accordance with the prescribed framework.The legislation also provides additional safeguards for children's data. Organisations are generally required to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing the personal data of children below 18 years. The law also restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, subject to specified exemptions.The framework provides for the Data Protection Board of India, which is responsible for examining complaints, conducting inquiries and determining penalties for non-compliance.The financial consequences can be significant. Under the Act, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach can attract a penalty of up to Rs 250 crore. Violations relating to breach notifications and obligations concerning children's data can attract penalties of up to Rs 200 crore.The most prominent concern raised by the DNPA is the absence of a specific exemption for journalistic activities.The association argues that the law does not adequately distinguish between the commercial processing of personal information and its use for reporting matters of public interest.Journalists frequently rely on personal information while investigating allegations involving public officials, companies, financial transactions and government decisions. Such investigations may require access to records and information without informing the person concerned in advance.For instance, a journalist investigating alleged irregularities in the assets of a public official may need to examine financial records, property details and business associations. Seeking consent from the individual before collecting or using such information could alert the subject to the investigation and potentially compromise the reporting process.Similarly, time-sensitive reporting and live television coverage often involve the use of information about individuals without obtaining prior permission.The DNPA has argued that the notice, consent and data-erasure requirements under the DPDP framework could make such activities difficult.In its petition, the association has challenged Sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act, along with Rules 16, 17 and 23 of the DPDP Rules.It has argued that the provisions fail to recognise journalistic activity as a distinct category deserving protection under the Constitution and could affect journalists, ground reporters, whistleblowers, citizen journalists and RTI activists.The association has also raised concerns over the possibility of individuals withdrawing consent and seeking erasure of their personal information. It fears that this could be used to pressure news organisations into removing reports or altering digital archives, even when the information is relevant to public interest.The challenge is not about denying individuals the right to privacy. Rather, it concerns whether the law provides sufficient safeguards for reporting that requires the collection and publication of personal information in the public interest.The debate has produced differing assessments of whether journalism needs a separate exemption under the legislation.Advocate Adhitya Srinivasan believes the constitutional protection enjoyed by the press and the nature of the legislation could allow competing interests to be resolved through judicial scrutiny."Freedom of press is so well-entrenched in our Constitution, so I really don't think that the DPDP Act is going to materially impair investigative journalism," Srinivasan said.He argued that Parliament had deliberately chosen a framework that articulates core principles without becoming overly prescriptive, leaving courts to undertake a balancing exercise when competing rights come into conflict."This is hardly unusual, and far from being problematic, it is just a deliberate choice that Parliament has made," he said.Srinivasan also pointed out that the legislation was not necessarily intended to restrict reporting. In his assessment, its objective could instead be to discourage practices such as doxxing and voyeurism.On the question of whether journalism requires an explicit exemption, he said: "I don't think journalism needs an explicit exemption under the DPDP Act, but I suppose it wouldn't hurt."Advocate Mayank Arora, however, takes a more cautionary view, arguing that the absence of an express exemption could create significant difficulties for public-interest reporting."I think yes, there is a strong likelihood that The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, could affect investigative journalism because it does not expressly exempt public-interest reporting from its consent requirements," Arora said.He argued that journalists investigating allegations involving public officials may need to examine financial records, ownership details and private communications, and seeking consent from the individuals concerned could defeat the purpose of an investigation.Arora also warned that the law could produce a chilling effect, with journalists avoiding investigations into powerful individuals because of potential complaints, litigation costs and regulatory uncertainty."The real danger here is not necessarily direct censorship, but a chilling effect on journalists," he said.He maintained that an explicit exemption would provide stronger protection for legitimate investigative reporting while preserving safeguards against misuse of personal information.Another major point of contention is Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005.The earlier provision allowed public authorities to withhold personal information if it had no relationship to public activity or interest, or if its disclosure would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy. However, it also allowed disclosure where a larger public interest justified making the information available.The amendment changes the wording of the exemption to cover information relating to personal information.Critics argue that the revised provision removes the earlier balancing mechanism between privacy and public interest, potentially making it more difficult for citizens to access information held by public authorities.The implications could extend to information concerning public officials, government decisions and the functioning of public institutions.For example, a journalist or an RTI applicant seeking information about the assets or official dealings of a public servant may encounter questions over whether the information falls within the personal information exemption.The central concern is that information could be withheld even when its disclosure has a legitimate bearing on public accountability.The government, however, has defended the amendment.In a PIB release issued on August 20, 2025, MeitY said the DPDP Act sought to recognise both an individual's right to protect personal information and the need to process such information for lawful purposes.The ministry maintained that the amendment to the RTI Act was intended to balance the right to privacy with the right to information.Srinivasan believes concerns over the amendment may be overstated."This suggestion that the RTI amendment weakens the right to access public information is in my view a red herring," he said.He argued that the amendment does not prevent public authorities from disclosing personal information when the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm."By way of the substitution, personal information cannot be given to citizens as a matter of right. This does not, however, stop a public authority from allowing access to information (even personal information) if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm," he said.Arora, on the other hand, believes the amendment substantially weakens the express public-interest protection previously available under the RTI Act.He pointed to cases involving recruitment records or alleged favouritism in government departments, where information could reveal corruption involving public money but may now be denied under the broader personal-information exemption.He also questioned why the earlier public-interest qualification was removed if authorities could continue to disclose information after weighing competing interests.The DNPA has also questioned provisions that give the government powers to seek information and restrict access to certain information.Section 36 empowers the Centre to call for information from Data Fiduciaries or intermediaries for specified purposes. The association has argued that the provision could affect the confidentiality of information held by news organisations.Journalists often depend on confidential sources, including whistleblowers and individuals who share information about alleged corruption, corporate wrongdoing or administrative irregularities.The possibility of sensitive information being sought by the government, the association argues, could discourage people from sharing information with journalists.This could have implications for investigative reporting, particularly when sources fear that their identities or communications may be exposed.Another provision under challenge is Section 37, which empowers the government to direct the blocking of access to information in specified circumstances.The association has questioned the scope of these powers and the safeguards available against their possible misuse.The broader concern is whether provisions intended to protect personal information could also create restrictions on the circulation of news and information.The composition and functioning of the Data Protection Board of India have also come under scrutiny.The Board is expected to serve as the principal adjudicatory institution under the law. It will examine complaints, conduct inquiries and determine penalties against organisations that fail to comply with the framework.However, questions have been raised about the government's role in the appointment of its members and the extent of its institutional independence.Under the notified rules, the selection process for the chairperson and members involves a search-cum-selection committee comprising senior government officials and government-nominated experts.The DNPA has challenged provisions concerning the Board, including Sections 18 and 19 of the Act and Rule 17 of the Rules.The concern is that an institution responsible for adjudicating disputes involving both private organisations and government departments should have adequate independence from the executive.Government agencies themselves process large amounts of personal information while implementing welfare schemes and providing public services. This makes the independence of the regulatory institution an important aspect of the data protection framework.The Centre has defended the legislation, maintaining that its primary objective is to protect citizens' privacy and regulate organisations that collect and process personal information.Union electronics and information technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has rejected suggestions that the law is intended to restrict journalistic freedom.On October 29, Vaishnaw said that freedom of the press was constitutionally guaranteed and that the government had no intention of affecting it.He also indicated that editors and media professionals could engage with the government to discuss their concerns.The government's position is that the obligations under the legislation are primarily directed at Data Fiduciaries, such as banks, telecom companies and insurance providers, rather than journalists as a category.In a report published on October 31, The Times of India quoted senior MeitY officials as saying that the Centre was open to changing the rules and, if necessary, the law itself to ensure that the framework did not become an impediment for journalists and media organisations.Officials maintained that journalists and media houses do not fall within the category of Data Fiduciaries merely because they undertake reporting activities.They also indicated that exemptions could be incorporated into the rules to address concerns over journalistic work.Arora, however, believes government assurances alone cannot provide adequate protection."Assurances must be backed by statutory provisions and enforceable laws and rules," he said.He argued that an express exemption would offer a stronger legal foundation for independent journalists and digital publishers, rather than leaving the matter dependent on administrative assurances.Although the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, the government has provided a phased implementation timeline to allow organisations to prepare for compliance.According to the enforcement timeline published by MeitY, certain institutional provisions, including those relating to the establishment of the Data Protection Board, came into force in November 2025.The amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act also came into effect as part of the initial phase.Other provisions, including the main obligations governing the processing of personal data, are scheduled to come into force 18 months after the November 13, 2025 notification. This places the key implementation date at May 13, 2027.The transition period is intended to give organisations time to establish consent mechanisms, strengthen security systems and put procedures in place to comply with the law.For news publishers, however, the legal uncertainty is likely to remain until the Supreme Court examines the challenge and the government clarifies whether additional exemptions will be introduced.The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on October 27 after hearing the DNPA's challenge. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana agreed to examine the petition and listed the matter for November 17.The court did not grant an interim stay on the challenged provisions without hearing the government's response.The Centre will now have to respond to the questions raised by the association, including the absence of a specific journalistic exemption, the amendment to the RTI Act and the powers granted to the government under the legislation.The government has also indicated that it is willing to consider changes if required.The outcome could have implications beyond news organisations. It may help determine how privacy rights, access to public information and the freedom to investigate are balanced under India's digital regulatory framework.The debate over the DPDP Act reflects a difficult balance between two important principles.On one hand, individuals should have control over their personal information. Financial details, health records, identity documents and private communications should not be freely collected, shared or used without appropriate safeguards.On the other, access to information and the ability to investigate matters of public interest are essential to accountability. Journalism and the RTI framework often require the examination of information that may be personal in nature but has wider public significance.The challenge, therefore, is not simply about choosing between privacy and press freedom. It is about creating safeguards that protect both without allowing one to become an obstacle to the other.The Supreme Court's examination of the law will be important in determining how these competing interests are reconciled.For citizens, the implications go beyond newsrooms and technology companies. They concern how much control individuals have over their personal information, how easily they can access information about public institutions and how effectively those in positions of authority can be held accountable.As India moves towards a more data-driven economy, the task before policymakers is to ensure that stronger privacy protections do not come at the cost of transparency and the public's right to know.
Article Summary: Parliament passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in August 2023. Legal challenge raises questions over how the law could affect investigative journalism, RTI access and government accountability. The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre and listed the matter for further hearing on November 17.

Article Title: Skill subject to offer class X Board students a second chance
Article Text:

Students may no longer have to fear failing the class X board exams as the CBSE has introduced a new rule that not only enhances the relevance of vocational education but also offers students an alternative pathway to pass. From 2027-28, students who fail a core academic subject such as Maths, Science or Social Science, will be allowed to use a passed skill subject as a substitute.This rule is only for students who have opted for one of the 22 skill subjects in class IX under vocational education. This excludes Kaushal Vikas, which is also a skill subject but is assessed internally by schools.Under the revised framework, class IX students will study nine subjects, combining core and skill-based courses. Vocational education includes 22 skill-based subjects, including AI, Data Science, Information Technology, Financial Markets, Automotive, Retail, Design Thinking, and Health Care.Under the NCF-SE, vocational education is mandatory from classes VI to X.A senior CBSE official says the goal is to expand choices for students and promote competency-based, experiential learning by embedding activity-based life skills alongside core academics.Class X students now have two attempts to pass CBSE boards in class X. If a student still cannot clear one core subject, this vocational component provides a cushion to clear class X and move to the next grade.A student who fails a core subject but passes class X through a skill subject can still sit for an improvement examination in the failed subject. CBSE does not have any regulation on which stream the student enrols in class XI as that is the school's discretion."Even if the student passes the boards using skill subject marks, he will have to pass Math or Science to enrol in science stream in class XI," adds the official.Teachers dismiss the idea that the replacement rule will dilute academic rigour, viewing it instead as a constructive stress buster. "This provision will help reduce examination stress, particularly among academically weaker students," says a teacher from PM SHRI KV NER Bareilly.
Article Summary: Students who fail a core academic subject will be allowed to use a passed skill subject as a substitute. This rule is only for students who have opted for one of the 22 skill subjects in class IX under vocational education. This excludes Kaushal Vikas, which is also a skill subject but is assessed internally by schools.

Article Title: Hijack hoax forces flight back to Bengaluru
Article Text: The discovery of a handwritten note threatening to hijack an IndiGo flight with 178 passengers aboard prompted the pilots to return to Bengaluru just 30 minutes after taking off for Lucknow Saturday evening. "The piece of paper (found in the toilet of the flight) carried the message: 'This plane is going to get hijacked exactly at 6.30. Ignore this and see the consequences.' Article Title: Ailing Kerala elephant calf, Maya, airlifted to Anant Ambani's Vantara for intensive hospitalisation
Article Text:
A crucial second opinion brings renewed hope

A collaborative model of compassionate care

Maya, an 18-month-old critically ill orphaned elephant calf, has been airlifted from Kerala’s Abhayaranyam to Anant Ambani's Vantara in Jamnagar for specialised intensive hospitalisation. The calf, who has been unable to stand following a severe fall in July, was shifted to the facility after medical experts sought advanced veterinary intervention as a final effort to prevent euthanasia. This life-saving transfer was initiated when Kerala officials explicitly requested the intervention of Vantara to explore every possible medical avenue.Maya's short life has already been a test of resilience. On April 19, 2025, she was found abandoned as a severely dehydrated newborn near Kaprikkad in the Malayattoor Division. Rescued and brought to Abhayaranyam, she was hand-reared around the clock by the Kerala Forest Department. Sadly, her struggles did not end there. On July 2, 2026, the calf slipped while playing and injured her right shoulder. Despite physiotherapy and dietary supplements, her condition rapidly deteriorated.By late October, she could no longer stand and was accepting only liquid feed. A thorough external examination revealed multiple fractures in her limbs, a chest infection, and generalised bone thinning. Faced with extremely brittle bones and a grave prognosis, a Medical Board made the heavy animal-welfare decision to recommend euthanasia on October 29 to prevent further suffering.Refusing to close the case, Kerala’s Chief Wildlife Warden, Dr. P. Pugazhendi, pursued a wider expert opinion before considering any irreversible actions. After reviewing her X-rays and blood work during a video consultation, Vantara’s veterinary experts identified a potential parathyroid-related disorder that could respond to treatment. With this new possibility, the decision was unanimously made on November 5 to transfer Maya to Vantara. At their facility, she will receive comprehensive pain management, advanced diagnostics, and support from hydraulic lifting systems to position her safely. Stepping in to provide this critical care, Vantara acted on the core principle of Anant Ambani: every life matters, driven by the philosophy of Jeev Seva.What makes this medical mission truly remarkable is the deep partnership built around the calf's emotional well-being. Before the journey, Vantara submitted a comprehensive treatment plan, and arranged an airlift equipped with life-support systems. To ensure Maya feels secure in an unfamiliar environment, the Kerala Forest Department has sent Assistant Forest Veterinary Officer Dr. Binoy C. Babu and her familiar caregiver, Shri Nikhil Babu, to accompany her on the flight.Crucially, her caregiver will remain by her side throughout the entire treatment period in Jamnagar to provide vital continuity. A Kerala Monitoring Committee will closely oversee her medical progress, and once the treatment is complete, Vantara will facilitate her return home to Abhayaranyam.The road ahead is undeniably difficult, and her prognosis remains uncertain. However, with two dedicated institutions working flawlessly together and familiar faces by her side, every conceivable effort is being made to give Maya the best possible chance.
Article Summary: Maya, an 18-month-old critically ill orphaned elephant calf, has been airlifted from Kerala’s Abhayaranyam to Anant Ambani's Vantara in Jamnagar. The calf, who has been unable to stand following a severe fall in July, was shifted to the facility after medical experts sought advanced veterinary intervention to prevent euthanasia.

The BJP is working to take forward both the heritage of this country and the legacy of the party,” he said.Nabin also described Advani as an example of the dignity, probity and sensitivity that politics should uphold.“I could not get an opportunity to work with him, but what I have heard from others who worked with him tells me that Advani's life has been an inspiration for everyone in BJP,” he said.He added that Advani had demonstrated immense dedication to the nation despite having experienced the pain of Partition.“He could take even hard decisions with simplicity,” Nabin said.Recalling Advani's role in the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, Nabin referred to the veteran leader's Ram Rath Yatra, which was stopped at Samastipur in Bihar.He said the slogan “We will build the temple right there” had been raised by BJP workers and crores of people across the country. Although the yatra was halted in Bihar, kar sevaks carried forward Advani's mission, he said.Nabin credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi with taking that journey forward, pointing to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya as a moment to remember Advani's contribution.“Today, as the country witnesses the magnificent Shri Ram Temple standing in Ayodhya, it is a moment for all of us to honour and remember Shri Advani Ji's historic journey,” he said.Senior Union minister and BJP treasurer Piyush Goyal also recalled his association with Advani, saying the veteran leader never made others feel the weight of his seniority or influence.He said party workers fondly called Advani 'dada' and that the leader had always treated him like a family member, addressing him by his nickname, 'Happy'.“Advani only thought about taking the country and taking the party forward with complete selflessness,” Goyal said, while wishing him a long life.“We all wish that this country continues to get a leader like Lal Krishna Advani,” he added.

Article Title: Rajasthan's local poll rolls have 30 lakh more voters than EC's final SIR list: Activist
Article Text:
In Rajasthan, a troubling disparity has emerged regarding the electoral rolls for local body elections, with the state election commission clinging to a voter list that dates back to January 2025.

Activist questions use of outdated voter lists

Nearly 30 lakh voters listed in electoral rolls used for local body elections in Rajasthan are absent from the election commission's final voter list following the Special intensive revision (SIR) exercise, a civil rights activist has alleged.According to news agency PTI, the discrepancy reportedly exists between the election commission's final SIR electoral roll and the voter lists maintained by the Rajasthan state election commission (SEC) for urban local body and panchayat elections.The SEC has attributed the difference to its continued use of the pre-SIR electoral roll, explaining that preparations for local elections had started well before the revision exercise was completed.According to Rajasthan's final SIR electoral roll, published in February 2026, the state's electorate declined from 5.47 crore to 5.15 crore. The revision resulted in the deletion of 44.28 lakh names and the addition of 12.91 lakh new voters.However, the SEC's electoral rolls covering the same 199 Assembly constituencies continued to carry approximately 5.45 crore names, creating a difference of nearly 30 lakh voters.SEC secretary Rajesh Verma said the commission had adopted the Election Commission's pre-SIR electoral roll, which was last updated on January 1, 2025, as the basis for preparing voter lists for local elections.He added that the SEC traditionally relies on election commission electoral rolls updated through the annual special summary revision process for local body polls.Chief electoral officer Naveen Mahajan also confirmed that the SEC had used the pre-SIR list. He said no objections had been received in Rajasthan against the final SIR electoral roll.Nikhil Dey, rights activist and founder of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, questioned the SEC's decision to continue using the older electoral roll despite the availability of the revised list.Dey argued that electoral rolls undergo regular updates and that the state election commission could have adopted the election commission's final SIR list instead.He also sought clarification on why the SEC considered its older voter list more reliable than the election commission's final version.Raising concerns over the apparent inconsistency, Dey questioned how booth-level officers could mark individuals as deceased in one electoral roll while their names continued to appear in another.A comparative analysis conducted by Dey found that 26.63 lakh voters whose names were removed during the SIR exercise were still listed in the SEC's 2026 electoral rolls for urban local body and panchayat elections.
Article Summary: Activist questions use of outdated voter lists in Rajasthan. State election commission clinging to a voter list that dates back to January 2025. Nearly 30 lakh voters listed in electoral rolls used for local body elections are absent from the election commission's final voter list following the Special intensive revision (SIR) exercise.

Article Title: 'First Diwali without Naxal terror': PM Modi celebrates with jawans in Bastar, targets Congress
Article Text:
The Prime Minister said that this is the first Diwali since the end of Naxalism in the region.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security personnel deployed in Chhattisgarh's Bastar region on Sunday. PM Modi credited the forces for their sacrifices in the fight against Left-wing extremism and took a dig at previous Congress governments, accusing them of failing to tackle the insurgency."Because of your sacrifices we have put an end to the terror of Naxalism here," PM Modi said while addressing the personnel.Addressing the gathering, PM Modi said he had come to celebrate the festival with the security personnel as a representative of the country's 140 crore citizens.Drawing a parallel between the responsibilities of soldiers guarding India's borders and security personnel fighting insurgency within the country, PM Modi said internal security was equally important for protecting the nation's unity and integrity."When a nation's internal security is strong, external enemies cannot succeed. However, when internal security is weakened, external enemies also begin to raise their heads," he said.The prime minister then turned his attention to the previous Congress-led governments, alleging that they had treated Naxalism as an incurable problem rather than taking decisive action against it."If you look at the figures from 2004 to 2013, you will find that every year, the number of our brave soldiers martyred was higher than the number of Naxalites killed.Unfortunately, the governments of that time treated Naxalism as an incurable disease and left it unaddressed," he said.Recalling the violence that had gripped Chhattisgarh for years, PM Modi cited the 2010 Dantewada attacks, in which 76 CRPF personnel were killed in an encounter with Naxalites and 44 civilians lost their lives in another incident."This land was soaked in the blood of our brave soldiers. But not a single voice of anguish was heard from those influential leaders living in their palaces. Not a single tear was shed by them," he said.The prime minister also spoke about his tradition of celebrating Diwali with security personnel, saying they were like family to him. He recalled previous celebrations with the forces, from Kargil and Lepcha in the Himalayas to Sir Creek and INS Vikrant.Bastar has remained at the centre of the government's campaign against Left-wing extremism, with the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Chhattisgarh Police playing a key role in anti-Naxal operations.On March 31, the government announced that the country had been freed from the menace of Naxalism following the elimination of several senior leaders and cadres, alongside the surrender of hundreds of others.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security personnel deployed in Chhattisgarh's Bastar region. PM Modi credited the forces for their sacrifices in the fight against Left-wing extremism. He took a dig at previous Congress governments, accusing them of failing to tackle the insurgency.

NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress MP Kirti Azad on Sunday hit out at the Bharatiya Janata Party ( BJP ) over its repeated references to the Ram Temple, accusing the party of using religious sentiments for political gains. He said he had visited the Kamakhya Temple but had never visited the Ram Temple in Ayodhya and had no intention of doing so in the future.His remarks come amid a political row over Samajwadi Party (SP) supremo and former Uttar Pradesh chief minister Akhilesh Yadav 's proposed visit to the Ram Mandir and Hanumangarhi temple in Ayodhya on December 12.The proposed visit has drawn criticism from the BJP, which has termed it a political exercise ahead of the elections and accused Yadav of seeking electoral mileage through visits to prominent religious sites.Speaking to news agency IANS, Azad questioned why the BJP repeatedly invoked the Ram Temple and accused the party of misusing temple donations."I do not understand why this Bharatiya Janata Party, which is involved in extortion and stealing donations, keeps talking about the Ram Temple. I have not visited the Ram Temple; I have visited the Kamakhya Temple. Are they suggesting that a person is not a Hindu if they worship Goddess Kamakhya? I worship Goddess Kamakhya, but I have not visited the Ram Temple," he said.Referring to Goddess Sita's birthplace and the episode of her Agni Pariksha, Azad questioned the circumstances surrounding her subsequent abandonment."I belong to the birthplace of Mata Sita. Mata Sita had to undergo the Agni Pariksha, and even after passing it, she was abandoned. Is it right for any human being to treat his wife this way -- to make her undergo the Agni Pariksha and then abandon her even after she passes it? This is not right. I visit Kamakhya Temple and Tripura Sundari Temple. Does that mean I am not a Hindu?" theTMC MP said.Reiterating his stand, Azad told IANS, "I have not gone to Ram Temple, nor will I ever go. I'll go to Mathura."He further accused the BJP of exploiting religious sentiments for political purposes and said the party had failed to establish the ideals of Ram Rajya in the country."They are doing this for politics and are orchestrating robberies and thefts at every temple. They do not have any other issue than Ram. The BJP has not brought Ram Rajya but Ravan Rajya in the country," he added.

Article Title: 'Engines failing': DKS accuses Centre of 'cover up' amid ethanol blending row
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Sunday targeted the Centre over allegations of excessive ethanol blending in petrol, claiming that thousands of vehicles were experiencing problems, including repeated engine failures and reduced mileage. He said the state government had collected samples from 67 locations and was investigating complaints about ethanol levels exceeding the prescribed limit."Engines are stopping repeatedly, and mileage has decreased," Shivakumar said, adding that around 30% of the investigation had been completed. He said the state government had already informed the Centre about the locations and that its findings would be made public."We have conducted an investigation first. 30% [of the work] is complete. Tomorrow, our Minister will officially hold a press conference and give all details. The government cannot cover it up," he said, as quoted by news agency ANI.Shivakumar alleged that excessive ethanol mixing was taking place at petrol pumps rather than during the supply process. "We have checked, and the mixing is happening at the petrol bunks.Where it is being distributed, mixing is happening there. We have all the documents," he said.Calling the issue a major concern for the country, the chief minister alleged that cheaper ethanol was being mixed with petrol to increase profits. "Because it is available at a lower price, they are mixing it to make a profit. We condemn this. It is dangerous. People need to be made aware and protected," he added.The remarks come amid a dispute between the Karnataka government and public sector oil marketing companies over allegations that petrol sold at some outlets in the state contained ethanol levels significantly higher than the prescribed 20% limit.Karnataka food, civil supplies, consumer affairs and legal metrology minister Rizwan Arshad had earlier said tests on samples collected from seven locations, including Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikkaballapura, Ramanagara, Mangaluru and Tumakuru, had recorded ethanol levels as high as 31.2%.However, Indian Oil Corporation Limited, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited rejected the allegations in a joint statement on Friday. The companies maintained that petrol supplied by them across the country, including Karnataka, complied with the Bureau of Indian Standards specification for E20 fuel.They also questioned the sampling procedure and testing methodology used in the state government's October 2026 exercise, arguing that the findings were based on third-party laboratory certificates that did not follow the prescribed statutory and technical procedures.
Article Summary: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar targeted the Centre over allegations of excessive ethanol blending in petrol. He claimed that thousands of vehicles were experiencing problems, including repeated engine failures and reduced mileage. The remarks come amid a dispute between the Karnataka government and public sector oil marketing companies.

NEW DELHI: AIMIM leader Waris Pathan has called for stronger Muslim political representation in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the upcoming assembly elections, asserting that the community would no longer remain confined to being a vote bank but would emerge as elected representatives and political leaders.Speaking to news agency ANI on Saturday, Pathan cited the electoral success of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, saying Muslims should aspire to occupy positions of political leadership and raise issues concerning the community and the poor. He also said that one day “Abdul” could become the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh and even the prime minister of India."Abdul has won. He will go to Vidhan Sabha. And he will become the voice of Muslims and poor people. He will fight for justice. And one day, Abdul will also become the Prime Minister of India. Remember my words. He can also become the chief minister of UP. Earlier, we said that he can also become the Mayor. Now there are so many corporate leaders. One day, Abdul will also become the chief minister of UP," Pathan said.Targeting those who allegedly use derogatory stereotypes against Muslims, Pathan said the community would no longer accept being reduced to such labels."In Michigan, Abdul has become a senator. He has won a historic victory. And the BJP people are using Abdul as a slur. They are passing derogatory remarks. That Abdul makes puncture. They are getting slapped. Now Abdul will not sit on the floor. Now Abdul will take part. Abdul will win. He will go to Vidhan Sabha," he said.Earlier on Wednesday, AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi had also criticised the BJP and the Samajwadi Party (SP), asserting that Muslims would no longer be treated as mere vote banks but would emerge as political leaders and lawmakers in Uttar Pradesh.Citing El-Sayed's electoral success in the US, Owaisi argued that Muslims have long been subjected to stereotypes in Indian political discourse."Abdul won in Michigan. Did this not become an issue when I said something on it? People from the BJP used to mock and say, 'Abdul puncture banata hai' (Abdul repairs punctures). The SP people used to say, 'Abdul dari bicchayega' (Abdul will spread the carpets)," Owaisi told ANI.Pathan also accused the BJP of discriminating against Muslims over their religious practices, food habits and places of worship, alleging that the community had faced growing hostility under the party's rule."Since the BJP government came into power in the last 12 years, they have completely ruined the country. Today, the BJP government has launched an open war against the Muslims. They hate our prayers, hijab, food, mosques, madrasas, bulldozers, mob lynching of Muslims," he said.He also criticised opposition parties, including the Congress and the SP, accusing them of approaching Muslims for electoral support without addressing their social, economic and educational concerns."Both parties have used the Muslims only for votes. They have done nothing else," he said.Referring to the Mahmood Rahman Committee and the Ranganath Mishra Commission reports, Pathan said their findings highlighted the community's socio-economic backwardness."The report of the Mahmood Rahman Committee is scary. Look at the report of the Ranganath Mishra Committee. All the reports are a testimony to the fact that the Muslims are backward," he said.Questioning the response of political leaders to issues concerning Muslims in Uttar Pradesh, Pathan asked whether they had visited families affected by demolitions or reached out to Muslim leaders who had been jailed."When the Muslims were oppressed in madrasas, where they were bulldozed, did you ever go there? When Azam Khan went back to jail, did you go to meet him?" he asked."The people are watching. They will get an equal answer in the elections," he added.Pathan also referred to the debate over Muslim population growth, arguing that the community's total fertility rate (TFR) had declined over the years."These numbers show that the total fertility rate of Muslims is decreasing. In 1992-1993, the Muslim's TFR rate was 4.4. It decreased to 2.6 in 2015-16. After that, it decreased to 2.3 in 1921. So the TFR rate is decreasing," he said.He accused certain political leaders of spreading misinformation and hostility towards Muslims, referring to remarks by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and a BJP MP on having three-four and four-five children."Why don't you stop them? And here, they are spreading lies. They are spreading hatred. They just want to defame the Muslims," he said.Urging people to refrain from making derogatory remarks against the community, Pathan said, "The people have become sensible. So stop talking nonsense."
Article Summary: AIMIM leader Waris Pathan has called for stronger Muslim political representation in Uttar Pradesh. He said Muslims would no longer remain confined to being a vote bank but would emerge as elected representatives and political leaders. Pathan cited the electoral success of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, saying Muslims should aspire to occupy positions of political leadership.
